cards.title: Addressing Chinese Air Force Seniors
cards.body: In China's air force, rank is crucial. Address seniors with their military title followed by their surname. Avoid using first names. When introducing yourself, use your rank and surname. Maintain a respectful and formal tone.
doThis: Use proper military titles and surnames
Be formal and respectful

source.doc: AFCLC Expeditionary Culture Field Guide: China (2025)

cards.title: Interacting with Local Civilians
cards.body: When interacting with local civilians, be mindful of their cultural norms. Use formal titles and surnames. Avoid public criticism or disagreement. Refuse requests politely and indirectly.
doThis: Use formal titles and surnames
Be polite and indirect

source.doc: AFCLC Expeditionary Culture Field Guide: China (2025)

cards.title: Respect Hierarchy in Meals
cards.body: Chinese meals often reflect hierarchy. Seniors or those of higher rank are seated first and served first. Wait for them to start eating before you begin. Use two hands when passing dishes to show respect.
doThis: Wait for seniors to start eating.
Use two hands when passing dishes.
avoidThis: Use one hand when passing dishes.

source.doc: AFCLC Expeditionary Culture Field Guide: China (2025)

cards.title: Save Face in Conversations
cards.body: Criticism or disagreement should be handled delicately to avoid causing someone to 'lose face'. Be polite and indirect. Use phrases like 'Perhaps we could consider...' instead of direct disagreement.
doThis: Use polite, indirect language.
Suggest alternatives gently.

source.doc: AFCLC Expeditionary Culture Field Guide: China (2025)

cards.title: Respecting Hierarchy
cards.body: Chinese culture values hierarchy and respect for seniors. When addressing superiors in the Chinese Air Force, use their titles and maintain a polite tone. Avoid direct disagreement or criticism.
doThis: Use formal titles when addressing seniors

avoidThis: Use first names or informal language with seniors

cards.title: Saving Face in Refusal
cards.body: Refusal is often indirect to save face. Instead of a direct 'no,' use phrases like 'It's difficult' or 'We'll try.' This approach maintains harmony and avoids embarrassment.
doThis: Use indirect phrases to refuse
Maintain a polite and harmonious tone
Offer alternatives or compromises
avoidThis: Criticize or blame others in refusal
Argue or insist on your point

cards.title: Navigating Checkpoints in China
cards.body: Checkpoints are common. Carry required documents. Be polite and patient. Avoid arguing with security staff to prevent losing face.

cards.title: Checkpoints and Radio Etiquette

cards.title: Navigating Refusal
cards.body: Chinese people may indirectly say no to avoid confrontation. They might say 'maybe', 'we'll see', or change the subject. Pay attention to non-verbal cues like hesitation or avoidance. If you need a clear answer, ask directly but politely.
doThis: Pay attention to non-verbal cues
Ask directly but politely for a clear answer
avoidThis: Assume a vague response means yes
Push for an answer if they seem uncomfortable

cards.title: Navigating Checkpoints Politely
cards.body: Chinese security staff value politeness and respect. Always greet them with a nod or a simple '你好 (nǐ hǎo)' and present your identification calmly. Avoid sudden movements or arguments to maintain a positive atmosphere.
